{{Short description|On sums of distances in triangles}}
[[File:Ungleichung erdos mordell2.svg|right|thumb|The Erdős–Mordell inequality illustrated]]
In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''Erdős–Mordell inequality''' states that for any triangle <math> ABC </math> and point <math> P </math> inside <math> ABC </math>, the sum of the distances from <math> P </math> to the sides is less than or equal to half of the sum of the distances from <math> P </math> to the vertices. It is named after [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Louis Mordell]]. {{harvtxt|Erdős|1935}} posed the problem of proving the inequality; a proof was provided two years later by {{harvs|last1=Mordell|first2=D. F.|last2=Barrow|year=1937|txt}}.{{sfnp|Mordell|Barrow|1937}} This solution was however not very elementary. Subsequent simpler proofs were then found by {{harvtxt|Kazarinoff|1957}}, {{harvtxt|Bankoff|1958}}, and {{harvtxt|Alsina|Nelsen|2007}}.{{sfnp|Kazarinoff|1957}}{{sfnp|Bankoff|1958}}{{sfnp|Alsina|Nelsen|2007}}

[[Barrow's inequality]] is a strengthened version of the Erdős–Mordell inequality in which the distances from <math> P </math> to the sides are replaced by the distances from ''P'' to the points where the [[angle bisector]]s of  <math> \angle APB </math>, <math> \angle BPC </math>, and <math> \angle CPA </math> cross the sides. Although the replaced distances are longer, their sum is still less than or equal to half the sum of the distances to the vertices.

== Statement and proof ==
Let <math>P</math> be an arbitrary point inside a given triangle <math>ABC</math>, and let <math>PL</math>, <math>PM</math>, and <math>PN</math> be the perpendiculars from <math>P</math> to the sides of the triangles.
(If the triangle is obtuse, one of these perpendiculars may cross through a different side of the triangle and end on the line supporting one of the sides.) Then the inequality states that{{sfnp|Alsina|Nelsen|2007}}
<math display="block">PA+PB+PC\geq 2(PL+PM+PN).</math>

The proof is as follows:
* Let the sides of <math> ABC </math> be <math> a </math>, <math> b </math>, and <math> c </math>, which are opposite to the vertices <math> A </math>, <math> B </math>, and <math> C </math>. Let us denote the distance between internal point <math> P </math> to all such three vertices as <math> PA = p </math>, <math> PB = q </math>, and <math> PC = r </math>, and the distance between internal point <math> P </math> to all three sides of a triangle <math> ABC </math>, namely the distance from <math> P </math> to <math> BC </math> is <math> x </math>, to <math> CA </math> is <math> y </math>, and to <math> AB </math> is <math> z </math>. First, we prove that <math display="block">cr\geq ax+by.</math> This is equivalent to <math display="block">\frac{c(r+z)}2\geq \frac{ax+by+cz}2.</math>
* The right side is the area of triangle ABC, but on the left side, <math> r + z </math> is at least the height of the triangle; consequently, the left side cannot be smaller than the right side. Now reflect <math> P </math> on the angle bisector at <math> C </math>. We find that <math> cr \ge ay + bx </math> for the reflection of <math> P </math>. Similarly, <math> bq \ge az + cx </math> and <math> ap \ge bz + cy </math>. We solve these inequalities for <math> r </math>, <math> q </math>, and <math> p </math>:<math display="block"> \begin{align} r &\geq (a/c)y+(b/c)x, \\
 q &\geq (a/b)z+(c/b)x, \\
 p &\geq (b/a)z+(c/a)y.\end{align}</math>
* Adding the three up, we get <math display="block">
    p + q + r
\geq
    \left( \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{b} \right) x +
    \left( \frac{a}{c} + \frac{c}{a} \right) y +
    \left( \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} \right) z.
</math>
* Since the sum of a positive number and its reciprocal is at least 2 by [[Inequality of arithmetic and geometric means|AM–GM inequality]], we are finished. Equality holds only for the [[equilateral triangle]], where <math> P </math> is its centroid.

==Another strengthened version==
Let <math> ABC </math> be a triangle inscribed into a circle <math> O </math>, and <math> P </math> be a point inside of <math> ABC </math>. Let <math> D </math>, <math> E </math>, and <math> F </math> be the orthogonal projections of <math> P </math> onto <math> BC </math>, <math> CA </math>, and <math> AB </math>. Points <math> M </math>, <math> N </math>, and <math> Q </math> be the orthogonal projections of <math> P </math> onto tangents to <math> O </math> at points <math> A </math>, <math> B </math>, and <math> C </math>, respectively. Then,
<math display="block"> PM+PN+PQ \ge 2(PD+PE+PF)</math>
Equality hold if and only if triangle <math> ABC </math> is equilateral.{{sfnp|Dao|Nguyen|Pham|2016}}{{sfnp|Marinescu|Monea|2017}}

==A generalization==
Let <math>A_1A_2...A_n</math> be a [[convex polygon]], and <math>P</math> be an interior point of <math>A_1A_2...A_n</math>. Let <math>R_i</math> be the distance from <math>P</math> to the vertex <math>A_i</math>, <math>r_i</math> the distance from <math>P</math> to the side <math>A_iA_{i+1}</math>, <math>w_i</math> the segment of the bisector of the angle <math>A_iPA_{i+1}</math> from <math>P</math> to its intersection with the side <math>A_iA_{i+1}</math> then{{sfnp|Lenhard|1961}}
<math display="block"> \sum_{i=1}^{n}R_i \ge \left(\sec{\frac{\pi}{n}}\right)\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \ge \left(\sec{\frac{\pi}{n}}\right)\sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i </math>

==In absolute geometry==
In [[absolute geometry]]  the Erdős–Mordell inequality is equivalent, as proved in {{harvtxt|Pambuccian|2008}}, to the statement
that the sum of the angles of a triangle is less than or equal to two right angles.{{sfnp|Pambuccian|2008}}
